strengths: The paper addresses a practical NLP question: how much labeled data is needed for specialized classifiers to match general language models. Studying learning curves and performance variability provides useful empirical value.

The experiments cover eight datasets, seven models, and several adaptation strategies. The substantial repetition—100 runs for encoder fine-tuning and typically 20 for other approaches—is a strength for investigating instability.

Dataset-specific learning curves and break-even tables expose substantial variation across tasks. The manuscript provides prompts, basic training settings, a code link, and explicit discussion of computational and evaluation limitations.
weaknesses: The central variance-adjusted break-even statistic is insufficiently defined. Section 3.2 gives no precise crossing rule, probability threshold, or interpolation procedure explaining the detailed sample counts in Table 2. Standard-deviation bands alone do not establish the claimed low probability of inferior performance. Consequently, the reported 100–200% and 1500% increases lack a reproducible statistical interpretation. Define the estimator and quantify uncertainty in the estimated crossings.

The annotation budget is not adequately accounted for. Section 3 creates a 20% validation split and uses early stopping, without explaining whether validation labels are included in, or constrained by, the advertised 10/100-example budgets. This directly affects the practical annotation claims. Additionally, two in-context examples per class require 28 examples for DB Pedia, so the protocol at nominal budgets below that number needs clarification.

The general-model baselines need stronger validation. One prompt developed on Mistral is reused across models, and in-context learning uses a single fixed demonstration count. As written, the BoolQ instruction in Table 1 asks whether a passage contains an answer, which differs from determining the answer to its yes/no question. The acknowledged Flan-T5 collapse on DB Pedia also needs context-length and truncation checks. These choices can materially shift the baseline and hence the estimated break-even point.

The conclusion that instruction-tuning on ten examples approaches full-data performance needs additional controls. Flan-T5 training is capped at 250 steps per epoch, while further training reductions for larger models are mentioned without complete specifications. These choices complicate interpreting flat learning curves as evidence that additional data has little value. Potential overlap between evaluation tasks and prior supervised instruction-tuning data is also unexamined.

Several conclusions exceed the reported evidence. Section 3.1 claims that at most 100 examples suffice on multiclass datasets against any model, but Table 2 reports AG News crossings of 350–550 examples against Flan-T5, increasing to 1100 with variance considered. Other comparisons require thousands of examples or never cross. The title and practical recommendations should reflect this conditional behavior. Claims that instruction-tuning offers an optimal resource trade-off also lack measured annotation and deployment costs.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear despite the code link. Section 3 describes evaluation across training sizes, whereas the limitations restrict ChatGPT to one size and ten runs, and the impact statement describes similar size restrictions for all large-model prompting experiments. The manuscript should reconcile these accounts and specify shared test subsets, exact checkpoints, LoRA settings, and output-to-label mapping. The unresolved budget accounting and statistical definition affect the central contribution sufficiently to warrant revision before a Findings recommendation.
